prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and its development into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part for B006 with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. Holst established the incretin effect and GLP-1 secretion and action in humans. Drucker defined GLP-1 and GLP-2 receptor biology and tissue actions and carried the translational concept. Knudsen's albumin-binding acylation is the step that gave liraglutide and semaglutide durable action and so turned a short-lived peptide into a medicine. The mechanism has been confirmed independently for decades, and large randomized trials show metabolic, cardiovascular and renal benefit. Maturity is not in question. Round 1 left one real question, whether the prize weight sits on discovery or on the discovery that made translation possible. I have decided it sits on both, because Physiology or Medicine rewards a change in medicine that rests on a physiological discovery, and the chain breaks without the acylation step. I do not add a second prize part. The three-person cap is already used, and no other shortlisted achievement is clearly ready to displace one of these names.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness and I have not found a way to remove it. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide was a necessary early step, and Habener, who is outside the supplied names, belongs to the same record. My trio omits both, and a reader could say it honours drug engineering over discovery. The committee has no primary documents on the Mojsov and Habener priority question, and my recollection is not a substitute for them. The Mojsov trio has the mirror weakness, since it leaves out the step that produced the drugs. I also accept that crediting Knudsen sets a precedent for industrial work, which is only defensible if applied consistently.

responses.point: Perlmann argues for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov because identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is a discovery contribution, while Knudsen's work is industrial development, and he asks that the citation be explicit about who is not credited.
responses.response: The distinction between discovery and development is a fair one, and it is the distinction I weigh differently. In my view the acylation work is not routine optimisation. It solved a specific physiological problem, the rapid inactivation of the peptide by DPP-4 and renal clearance, and it did so by an understanding of albumin binding. I accept your point that without Mojsov the active form is not known. But a prize that credits the active peptide and stops there celebrates a molecule that was not itself a therapy. I have not changed my view on this, though your argument has made me regard the Mojsov trio as fully defensible. I would support your request that the citation name the physiology and the development explicitly, so that the omissions are visible and not hidden.

responses.point: The chair moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, persuaded that the prize should centre on the biology and active molecular form of the hormone, and asks whether the committee will apply the same translation principle to B004 and B040.
responses.response: I understand why you moved, and I do not think that you were wrong to. On your question about consistency, my answer is that the principle I use is narrower than 'translation deserves credit'. I credit a development step only where it solved a defined biological problem and without it there is no medicine, as with acylation in B006. By that test B040 is harder to defend as a discovery prize, because the kinase target was defined first and the compound development followed from it. B004 passes more clearly, but there the attribution is cut by Eshhar's omission, so I keep it as an alternative and not as a second part. If the committee rejects this principle, then the Mojsov trio is the coherent choice and I would not oppose it as strongly as my ranking might suggest.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius also names Drucker, Holst and Knudsen and wants the citation to state both the physiology and the development into long-acting therapy, while noting that the clinical field is still moving. She ranks B028 (cGAS-STING) above B039 among alternatives.
responses.response: We agree on the trio and the citation, and I share your concern that crediting an industrial step stretches the prize toward drug development. The field still moving is not a reason for delay here, in my view, because the long-acting analogues have a decade of outcome data and the later agents extend the same mechanism and do not replace it. On the alternatives I still differ. I put B039 ahead of B028 because its mechanism is established across several decades with a compact credit, whereas for cGAS-STING the clinical and physiological consequence is still largely inferred. I would revisit that order in a later year, but for now I do not think the cGAS-STING case is ready to carry a second part.

responses.point: Sandberg would accept swapping Mojsov for Knudsen if the citation named the therapeutic achievement and notes that whichever trio is chosen can be criticised for either excluding drug development or privileging a disputed priority claim.
responses.response: Your statement that either trio can be criticised is the most honest summary of the problem, and I agree with it. Your willingness to accept Knudsen if the citation names the therapeutic achievement is why I think the committee can converge on wording that includes both physiology and development. I would not expect the committee to resolve the Mojsov and Habener priority question by argument, as none of us has the documents. For that reason I would choose the configuration whose omission can be explained in the citation by a clear principle, and mine rests on a stated test rather than on a priority ruling that we cannot verify.

uncertainties: Mojsov and Habener priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide: I rely on recalled history and have not seen primary documents, so I cannot rule on it.

Whether the committee will accept the principle that a development step may be credited only when it solves a defined biological problem, and whether that principle can be applied evenly to B004 and B040.
Whether B039 or B004 would be a more suitable second part in a later year, and how Eshhar's omission and the other UPR contributors would be handled.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. My documented connections are a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, work with Patrik Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, none involving a shortlisted candidate or credited name. B037 (optogenetics) is in my own field of neuroscience, but I list no personal tie to its candidates and it is not in my configuration.
